Gold first, games after

On the waiting screen the shop comes before the toy box: showcase,
pre-registration and appointment booking sit directly under the ticket,
the entertainment tiles follow below them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The toy box stands where the waiting customer actually looks

The game tiles rendered only in the queue detail view - a page most
customers never open. The home screen, where the ticket number lives,
never showed them, so a switched-on feature was invisible in practice:
server said yes, code said yes, screen said nothing. The tiles now sit
directly under the ticket card on the home screen too, and disappear the
moment the customer is called, same as before.

Six staff-panel explanations traded insider shorthand for plain words:
what the serial toggle is for, what the vault-readiness view actually
checks, what auto mode does and when it steps aside, and the register's
question asked the way a clerk would ask it. The trade's own terms stay
where the trade needs them.

The customer page speaks customer, in five languages

A visitor asked what a counter is, and rightly so: the proof page talked
about deals, hashes and anchoring - our words, not theirs. Sixteen
customer-facing texts now say it plainly: an anonymous verification
number instead of a hash key, your receipt checked against the original
instead of recomputed anchors, come to the till instead of the counter,
report a loss and every dealer using the register sees it. Staff screens
keep the trade's language; the customer never needed it.

The intro now names the Confidential Compute case in one breath: the
stolen-goods question two parties must answer without showing their data,
the extension for it registered on Coston2, and the wallets that retire
the operator's last key. A reader knows within ten lines why this sits in
the Confidential Compute track.

The unlock clock reaches the schema a reviewer boots

The pushed registry code already knows that clearing a loss report takes
time or an ID - clear_requested_at and ever_reported_at - but the schema a
fresh docker loads did not have the two columns yet, so the reviewer path
broke exactly where the README sends it. The asymmetry they implement is
deliberate: reporting is instant, clearing waits out a delay unless
management saw an ID, because a wrong report is a conversation and a wrong
clearance is the loss.

The demo scale weighs the piece on it - to the milligram

A fixed number in the simulator gave a Maple Leaf the weight of a
Krugerrand and disproved the demo it was built for. The simulated scale
now asks, on every tick, what the requested row expects, settles anew when
the piece changes, and reports to 0.001 g the way a real precious-metals
counter scale does - so the display meets the catalogue value instead of
rounding past it. The gate got a dead-man timeout too: a scale that stops
sending must fail the run, not end it looking green.

Auto mode calls one buyer at a time - and says why it parked the rest

A called buyer waiting to be paid counted as parked work, so the desk
called the next customer, and the next: three people standing at one
counter. The question is not who handed a case over but whether a customer
is standing at the desk - ID checks, PEP reviews, payout limits and a
called buyer all block the next call-up now, while genuinely parked work
(missing items, missing price, a mail-in offer) waits for nobody. Where
auto mode puts a case down it leaves the reason on the tile, in all five
languages, instead of an amount that never came. And the demo scale weighs
what the requested row expects - not always a Krugerrand.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01PvkRN5N3wLU55PKg98PQqR

Every house seals under its own name

The anchor contract is write-once, and until now every installation derived
the same reference - keccak of paigold:type:id. So the demo, a reviewer's
docker and the pilot all claimed the same numbers, and whoever came second
got an eternal "already anchored" without ever sending a transaction; the
retry button could not change that. References now carry the house name
(flare.anchor_namespace, defaulting to the host the installation answers
under), so no two houses ever share one. Seals set before the change stay
readable - both references are checked in order, only the new one is ever
written - and a foreign checksum found under our reference is reported as a
collision instead of being shown as our seal.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01PvkRN5N3wLU55PKg98PQqR

Typed in branch currency, booked in the deal's, judged in euros

A euro deal viewed at a dollar branch could deadlock the desk: the board
checked the booked euros against the AML threshold (below - so it hid the
two check boxes), while closing checked the raw display number (above - so
it demanded boxes that existed nowhere). And the payout would have booked
the dollar figure as euros, eight percent too much in the day's ledger.
Now the same arithmetic runs everywhere: amounts are typed in the branch
currency (the field says so), booked in the deal's own currency, and the
AML threshold always judges the euro value - in set_offer, complete and on
the board alike. The boxes appear exactly when closing will demand them.

Unlocking takes time or an ID - and the desk survives the odd paths

The owner key and the serial live on the same slip of paper, and a burglar
takes the safe with both. Until today that slip could lift a theft report the
morning after the theft. Now the key only REQUESTS the withdrawal: the block
stays, visibly, and falls after a grace period (7 days, configurable) - or
immediately at the counter, where management has seen an ID and the audit log
gets a line. Locking stays instant; the asymmetry is the point: a wrong block
is an argument, a wrong unlock is the loss. A lifted report stays visible as
history. The e2e gate grew from 24 to 34 checks, including the expiring clock
and the employee who may not lift a block.

Also two counter fixes found in live use, each with its own gate: serving a
ticket whose deal was no longer on the board white-screened the whole desk
(a placeholder object reached the modal), and manually assigning a waiting
customer to a room made him vanish from all three columns at once.

The conduit into the enclave: the register can now ask its question outside the house

REPORT_LOST, CLEAR_LOST - and reg_ask() tries the enclave before answering

counter with a waiting customer must never hang on a wire. What crosses the

politely without a running extension (26 checks with one), and verify.php
grew the corresponding check. FCC-INTEGRATION.md now records what is actually
buildable against the public scaffold instead of what we hoped in July.

Serial register: the question before the money

A dealer who buys stolen goods does not become the owner. So the counter
now asks one question before the valuation, and gets yes or no.

Three values kept apart on purpose: the serial is the common denominator,
the lookup value (HMAC with a house key) is what the register searches,
and the ownership key handed to the buyer authorises a report — never a
search. A first draft searched by the ownership key; building it showed
the dealer at the counter never has it.

The receipt is written for both answers. That is the point: it lets a
house show later that it looked.

Owners report a loss on the proof page with no account and no name.
Spelling does not matter. The serial never leaves the house.

reg_ask() is the single seam where the enclave takes over. The FCC doc
gains that status plus two corrections: the query value, and the claim
that Flare's indexer must be requested — the scaffold ships one and the
indexer is public.

Gates: _t_registry.php 25/25, _t_registry_e2e.cjs 24/24, verify.php 29 PASS.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

FCC doc: correct the status and say what is actually buildable today

The July version of this document said Confidential Compute was "not yet open
to developers". That stopped being true: the on-chain building blocks
(TeeExtensionRegistry, TeeMachineRegistry, InstructionSender) shipped in March
2026, guides and example extensions exist, and testing runs on Coston2 — the
same network this project already anchors to. Flare still calls FCC "in the
final stages of development and not yet a fully public production system", and
the document now says exactly that instead of something older and rosier.

New section 8 replaces guesswork with the documented path: an extension is a Go
HTTP server inside a TEE, run as three Docker services; local development works
without Confidential VM hardware via SIMULATED_TEE; the one prerequisite that
depends on somebody else is indexer access, granted on request.

It also names the smallest honest extension for this product — the stolen-goods
question from section 7, where the commitment already exists at the point of
sale — and separates what a simulated TEE can demonstrate from what needs the
real one. A toy that runs beats ten pages of seam; the seam stays right either
way, because it describes where the toy belongs.

A proof suite a reviewer can run: php verify.php, no setup, no network

Turns the claims in this README into a command anybody can execute.
28 checks, exit 0 when green:

- keccak256 known-answer tests, and the 4-byte selector derived from them
- RFC-6979 determinism, r/s inside the curve order, and the address for
  private key 1 compared against the public vector — checking the shape
  alone would let a broken derivation pass
- an EIP-155 transaction built and its v field decoded out of the RLP:
  264 = 114*2+35+recId, so Coston2's chain id is proven to be inside the
  signature rather than found somewhere in the hex
- five languages key for key, with the same {placeholders} in each
- print templates resolve to the Flare explorer, not to us
- no seal key in the versioned configuration

On top of it the domain gates run in the same call — 89 assertions with
no database and no network: why density alone misses a tungsten core, why
an advert never receives a draft reply, why a troy ounce is not an ounce.
The cryptography shows the arithmetic works; those show the trade is
understood.

The counter measures: scale, inspection report, transport, mail-in purchases — and seals that outlive a change to their own payload

- Scale read over WebSerial: weight goes from the device into the field and
  into the report, with device and timestamp. Troy vs. avoirdupois ounce kept
  apart. Parser gate 23/23, no hardware needed.
- Inspection report: twelve methods with device, reading, inspector, time —
  and the software names what is still missing. Density is not accepted as
  core evidence (tungsten 19.25 vs. gold 19.32); XRF only sees the surface.
  Sealed, recomputed on every read, A4 certificate with explorer QR. 23/23 + 19/19.
- Transport with a third audience: two seals (departure, acceptance), the
  second chaining the first. The carrier opens a page with bags, weights and
  seals — no customer data, no amounts. Weight beyond tolerance is recorded as
  disputed, not accepted. 21/21.
- Mail-in purchases: weight while still sealed plus a photo, anchored before
  anyone values anything. 15/15.
- Mail agent: reads over IMAP, classifies with reasons, writes drafts into the
  Drafts folder. No SMTP path exists and none can be enabled. 32/32 + 17/17.
- Books: a day counts cash out and metal in; shifts and closings run by
  themselves. Manager figures: gross profit per metal and per staff member,
  conversion rate, turnaround, days on hand — allocation stated in the answer.
- Vault items marked issuable when a claim would have everything it needs.
  Nothing is issued: that is MiCA territory, a company decision, not a switch.
- Payload versioning: adding one field on Aug 4 made 59 of 61 historical
  hand-overs read "does not match". Verification now walks all recipes, newest
  first, and reports which one matched; an anchor already on chain is never
  re-hashed. Gate 11/11 reproduces that day.
- Tool bar: fifteen buttons became six groups; mail and mail-in purchases are
  within the agent's reach.

Machines at the counter: auto mode, five languages, currencies that convert

Since the agent role landed, the desk was tested against real deals for
two days. What came out of it:

AUTO MODE. The API agent needs a model on the other end of a wire. Most
of a buy desk does not: inspect, offer, call, pay out, bag, seal, receipt
is the same chain every time. Auto mode runs it server-side, one step
every three seconds so a human can follow, with the card framed red while
a machine has it. No model, no outside connection, no cost per deal - and
the same limits as the agent. While a handover waits, the whole desk holds
still; it used to fetch the next customer and stack the approval cards.

THE HANDOVER IS A MOMENT. One full-screen card, the reason in plain
language, and the deal waits. After the payout the machine notices by
itself and continues with bagging, sealing, receipt. Cancelled deals stop
asking - thirteen old ones once kept auto mode waiting forever.

MACHINES ARE NOT ROLES. Signing in AS the agent is not an agent being
CONNECTED. Only sessions from "connect" carry the link marker, so the lamp
means what it says and the payout limit binds the machine, not the person
who sits down to take over. That one cost two rounds: the human who was
meant to approve a payout was blocked by the agent's own limit.

CURRENCIES. Eight, picked from a flag list, computed through the Metals &
FX oracle. The agent limit and the AML thresholds convert with them - a
fixed 10k EUR compared against a yen amount is a different rule in every
currency. Amounts keep the currency they were booked in.

LANGUAGES. Chinese and Japanese, 741 keys each, counter and customer app.

FIXES: silver priced as gold; the seal invisible to anyone who had not
clicked it; a paused agent that could not read its own state and hung the
desk in a loop of 423s; Authorization: Bearer dropped by Apache, so a
correct token answered "not signed in"; refinery.php missing from a
deployment; two print windows per deal where one belongs.

DOCKER: gmp/bcmath for the signer, setenvif for the bearer header, and the
schema now carries what the running code used to create for itself - a
fresh database is complete instead of becoming complete through use.
Verified end to end on a wiped volume.

Vault storage: deposits sealed on-chain, release chains the deposit hash - plus the silver-as-gold pricing fix

New module: vault storage. Dealers who store customer valuables hand
out paper certificates audited once or twice a year; on-chain
competitors tokenize ownership instead. PaiGold seals the deposit
itself: customer profile (AML), condition photo (its SHA-256 goes into
the anchor), condition grade, compartment and notes - anchored as
vault_in with the same live sent->sealed moment as the security bags.
Hand-back writes vault_out, whose payload chains the stored deposit
hash, framing the whole storage period on-chain. Deposit and release
receipts each carry a QR to their own transaction plus signature
lines. Values are computed, not typed: weight x fineness x the daily
rate from the own oracle, shown as "current value"; a declared value
remains only for pieces without metal data. A running deal can hand
its customer and goods into a prefilled deposit form (take into
storage). The table self-creates on first use, demo stock is one
click, and the landing page explains the module in plain language in
DE/FR/EN.

Pricing fix: a 100 g silver bar was suggested at EUR 10,386.39 - the
exact gold-spot arithmetic - because items without a catalogue link
fell back to a hard-coded 'gold' and two write paths never stored the
catalogue id. Metal now resolves centrally (catalogue -> inventory ->
description heuristic -> gold), is shown and overridable per item at
inspection, and the inspection prints its arithmetic per position
(metal, unit price x quantity = total). The AML tier reacts to the
suggested sum immediately, and the demo walk-ins became a curated AML
ladder (>=2k ID case, >=10k enhanced case, a genuine silver case, a
mixed cart). Guarded by a DB-less pricing gate, 17/17.

Also fixed: input_string() misuse - the third parameter is the
required flag, not a max length, so optional fields (compartment,
release note) had silently become required.

Landing: the vault section sells the dealer benefit (recurring fees,
no hand-back disputes, a receipt no bank offers) instead of listing
captured fields; vault joined the hero enumeration and the feature
grid (plus a branch-currency card); the rigid four-step "how a
purchase flows" section is gone - real counters differ; and the
receipt mockup now shows current arithmetic (1 oz gold ~3,233 EUR,
1 oz silver ~46 EUR) instead of stale prices.

Build log, Aug 1: branch currencies from the own FX feeds, catalogue at 130, seal journal export

Every branch trades in its own currency, priced by the own oracle

The FX half of the Metals & FX oracle was feeding the chain and nobody was
using it. Now it carries the till: a branch picks its currency in the admin
panel - EUR, USD, GBP, CHF, JPY, AUD, CAD or CNY, exactly what the oracle
covers - and everything follows at once: spot ticker, showcase, offers,
inspection pricing, scrap calculator, number formatting in both apps (JPY
gets its zero decimals from Intl, not from a special case).

How it works: flare_fx_factor_eur_to() converts via the own on-chain feeds
(EURUSD and CCYUSD, fresh within 2h; ECB as fallback; on failure the branch
stays in EUR rather than pricing off a stale factor). Stored spot prices
remain EUR-based - the single source of truth - and conversion happens in
the price engine; manual spot entry is typed in the branch currency and
converted back on save. The historical field name 'eur' now carries the
branch-currency amount when one is set ('ccy' says which). The column
self-creates on first save (MariaDB IF NOT EXISTS), so existing installs
need no migration step. Verified live against mainnet: EUR->USD 1.15,
GBP 0.852, CHF 0.927, JPY 115, CNY 7.67 - all from the own contract.

Accounting in one click grew a third export: the seal journal. Next to the
Excel/SKR03 sheet and the DATEV posting batch (format 7 - it earned its

The sealing moment works on shared hosting: PHP signs the anchor itself

Sealing a bag depended on a local Node service holding the key. On shared
hosting that service does not exist, so the counter always fell back to
"will be sealed later" — the sealing moment was unreachable in production.

blockchain/flare-signer.php removes the dependency: keccak256, secp256k1
with RFC-6979 deterministic k, RLP and an EIP-155 transaction, in plain PHP
with GMP or BCMath, no library. Verified against ethers v6 down to the byte
(hash vectors, selectors, address, r/s/v, full signed transaction, 14/14,
~10 ms per signature) and against the chain: an anchor written from PHP
alone, block 33479365, verify() returning a match.

The desk now shows the whole thing: transaction sent (hash + explorer link)
-> poll for the block -> sealed, with the block number. The server answers
immediately and the wait happens in the browser, so a hosting timeout can
no longer swallow a transaction. Off by default; an operator switches it on
with two config values, and an admin self-test reports extension, chain,
wallet, funding, authorisation and how many seals the balance still covers.

Mobile and the till itself:
- Phone layout for the desk. The KPI row was hidden behind sm: and the tools
  scrolled off the edge, so a clerk saw almost nothing. Now a compact figures
  row and one Menu sheet with every tool as a labelled tile, driven by the
  same list the desktop bar uses.
- The board dropped from five columns to three stages: waiting room &
  appointments / being served / completed. Queue tickets and today's
  appointments live on the board instead of behind a modal, each card with
  exactly one action: Serve (claim, inspect and open in one click) or Call.
- Call is a state change, not a highlight: the ticket leaves the queue, so
  the same customer can no longer stand in two places at once. No-shows can
  be dropped without inventing a deal first.

Every QR points at the chain: once a bag is sealed, the QR on screen, on the
customer receipt, the hand-over slip, the bag sticker and the proof sheet
all resolve to the transaction in the Flare explorer; the private proof code
stays alongside as a separate line. Checked by executing the print templates
and reading the URLs they emit (7/7), sealed and unsealed.

The post-payout checklist follows what physically happens: bag the goods ->
put the bag on the blockchain -> print the hand-over slip (carrying the real
transaction) and have it signed -> print the customer receipt. Paper is
created after the seal exists. "Bag into the vault" is no longer a step, and
a sealed bag offers no second seal — the registry is write-once.

Smaller repairs: print windows carry a way back (dismissing the print dialog
on a phone used to strand you inside the receipt), the customer proof page
has a back button, and a demo button seeds four random walk-ins so the flow
